hints: Focus on that low sublimation temperature of 178 °C, what does that tell you about ionic versus covalent bonding?
Remember that Al in $\text{AlCl}_3$ has only six electrons around it, so it wants to accept a lone pair to complete its octet by joining to another molecule.
Look for the $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ dimer with two bridging Cl atoms, and check the dative bond arrows point from the donor to the acceptor.
walkthrough:
**Use the sublimation temperature as a clue**

Solid $\text{AlCl}_3$ sublimes at only 178 °C. That is far too low for a giant ionic lattice like $\text{Al}^{3+}(\text{Cl}^-)_3$.

Low temperature means weak intermolecular forces, so the vapour must be simple covalent molecules.

**Recall why aluminium chloride dimerises**

A single $\text{AlCl}_3$ molecule is electron deficient. Al has only 3 bonds, so 6 electrons, not an octet.

$$2\text{AlCl}_3 \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$$
In the vapour, two molecules join together. Each Al accepts a lone pair from a Cl on the other molecule to reach 8 electrons.

**Pick the correct dimer with correct dative bonds**

The dimer has 4 terminal Cl atoms and 2 bridging Cl atoms shared between the two Al atoms.

The bridges are coordinate (dative covalent) bonds, so the arrow must point from the Cl lone pair donor to the Al acceptor. That matches the structure with two Al centres linked by two Cl bridges with arrows into Al.

options.A: Correct. This is $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ with two bridging Cl atoms. Each bridge donates a lone pair to the other Al, shown by arrows pointing from Cl to Al, giving every Al a full octet and tetrahedral arrangement.
options.B: Incorrect. This shows the right $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$ connectivity but the dative bond arrows are reversed. Arrows must go from electron donor (Cl) to electron acceptor (Al), not from Al to Cl.
options.C: Incorrect. This is the monomer $\text{AlCl}_3$. At around 178 °C the vapour is mainly the dimer $\text{Al}_2\text{Cl}_6$. Monomer only dominates at much higher temperatures when the bridges break. It also leaves Al with an incomplete octet.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{Al}^{3+}(\text{Cl}^-)_3$ suggests fully ionic bonding. An ionic lattice would have very high melting and boiling points, not sublime at 178 °C. Aluminium chloride is covalent due to polarisation by the small, highly charged $\text{Al}^{3+}$ ion.
